The Mountain ground squirrel (Geosciurus princeps) is a burrowing sciurid rodent native to montane grasslands of southern Africa. Under a stable core body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], the gestation period lasts approximately 46 days [tg = approximately 46 days], a duration typical of ground-dwelling squirrels of this body size. Newborns emerge at a wet weight at birth of approximately 20 grams [Wwb = approximately 20 grams], a value estimated from data on the closely related Cape ground squirrel, Geosciurus inauris. This altricial neonatal state necessitates continued maternal care within the natal burrow during the earliest weeks of life.

Juvenile development proceeds through a period of nursing followed by nutritional independence. At the same thermal regime of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], weaning is completed at approximately 28 days after birth [tx = approximately 28 days after birth], after which the young squirrel begins foraging on seeds, grasses, and invertebrates alongside other colony members. This delay allows young individuals to accumulate the somatic reserves and social standing necessary within the colony hierarchy before engaging in reproductive behavior. Reproductive output in this species is modest, with a maximum of one to three pups produced per litter and a single litter typically raised each year at the same reference temperature. Longevity in the Mountain ground squirrel reaches a maximum of approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years] at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], a lifespan consistent with the moderate pace of life typical of medium-sized, colonially burrowing sciurids.
